prompt.context:
RDTC is a large public accounting firm with over $3B in revenues and over 8,000 employees. Over the past three years the firm has been working to overcome challenges identified in their practice through an organization-wide change initiative. There are two key components of this change initiative—a brand new technology called LCS and a suite of tools, resources, and methodologies to ensure streamlined processes called RDTC Project Management. RDTC Project Management (RDTC PM) is the driving force behind the new RDTC Methodology to performing audits while LCS is simply the new software that will allow auditors to successfully execute this new methodology. This is also the first time in the history of the organization that project management has been emphasized and used to evaluate performance of staff.

RDTC is entering the third year of this change initiative and is at a critical inflection point with both LCS and RDTC PM. LCS has rolled out to all of the small and medium project teams but is now set to deploy to all large accounts. These large accounts bring in the most revenue for RDTC, have the largest teams, require the most staff hours, and have most senior audit partners leading them.

Deployment of RDTC PM has had several challenges. One of the most important aspects has been the role creation and hiring of 50 new, full-time project managers to enhance RDTC's project management capabilities; thereby ensuring a consistent methodology for performing audits. RDTC forecasted that the 50 new project managers would be assigned to the 70 largest project teams by this year. So far only 20 have been hired and assigned to 30 project teams. In addition, the existing project managers have met resistance from the account teams who are not accustomed to having project management oversight.

The adoption of this change initiative is essential to ensuring that RDTC stays competitive in the market and avoids penalties from the oversight board.
prompt.question: Develop a plan for the next year of RDTC's change initiative. Address the following: (1) How do we prioritize the challenges that the change initiative is facing? (2) What should RDTC consider as LCS prepares to deploy to large engagements? (3) How can RDTC attract new project managers and ensure the success of existing ones?

clarifying_info.q: When was the last time RDTC updated its software?
clarifying_info.a: They have been operating on their legacy system for the past 15-20 years, so not recently.

clarifying_info.q: How successful was the LCS rollout to small and medium engagements?
clarifying_info.a: It was met with a lot of resistance from audit personnel. To convert to LCS, engagement teams are supposed to submit software conversion requests. Teams consistently missed deadlines to submit conversion requests.

They are organized in regional divisions—East, West, and Central. Each region has the same leadership structure with one regional president, VP, and office leads. The project teams' clients are all within their region. Project Managers are supposed to be assigned to project teams within their region, but because there is a shortage many have had to work with teams outside of their region.

clarifying_info.q: What slowed the hiring of new project managers?
clarifying_info.a: Several things have slowed progress: (1) the career path for new project managers is not fully established, reducing attractiveness; (2) training has not been fully developed so leadership is not comfortable hiring additional PMs; (3) the opportunity has not been communicated across the organization; (4) currently only recruiting internally from experienced auditors who desire a career change, but could be open to outside candidates.

clarifying_info.q: Is there anything preventing them from hiring new project managers right now?
clarifying_info.a: They are waiting until the end of busy season to hire additional project managers. They will not be able to hire anymore for six months.

clarifying_info.q: Is engagement team leadership bought in to this initiative?
clarifying_info.a: Because senior managers, partners, and directors are accustomed to legacy technology, many have not submitted requests to convert to LCS and are reluctant to do so. Many do not understand the benefits of project management or the purpose of project managers. There are a few champions within the organization, but everyone is not aligned on what this change means.

framework: People: Leadership alignment, stakeholder buy-in, change curve prioritization
People: Recruitment and onboarding of new project managers (career path, training, communications)
People: Learning and development resources for engagement teams without a PM
Processes: Strategic communications plan for both LCS and RDTC PM rollout
Processes: How to handle 40 project teams still without an assigned project manager; PM utilization
Technology: LCS deployment strategy for large engagements—pilot, phased rollout, super users / train-the-trainer
Consider developing a Center of Excellence for both areas of the change initiative

questions.prompt: How do you prioritize the challenges the change initiative is facing?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will segment challenges by People, Process, and Technology (or similar MECE buckets). They should note that leadership alignment is the most critical—if senior partners are not bought in, neither LCS adoption nor PM oversight will succeed. A change-curve lens is useful: identify who is most resistant and who are the champions, then target energy accordingly. The candidate should avoid framing this purely as a technology adoption problem and recognize the organizational change dimension.

questions.prompt: What should RDTC consider as LCS prepares to deploy to large engagements?
questions.guidance: Key considerations: (1) Large accounts are highest-revenue and led by the most senior, most resistant partners—the stakes of a failed rollout are highest here. (2) Lessons from small/medium rollout: teams missed conversion request deadlines, so a tighter deadline enforcement or change in the request process is needed. (3) Recommended approach: perform a pilot with a willing large engagement first; use a phased rollout rather than simultaneous deployment; identify 'Super Users' or apply a 'train-the-trainer' philosophy to build internal capability and reduce perceived burden on senior partners. (4) Communications: proactively communicate benefits to senior partners before deployment.

questions.prompt: How can RDTC attract new project managers and ensure success of existing ones?
questions.guidance: Attraction side: (1) Establish and publicize a clear career path for the PM role; (2) Expand recruiting beyond internal experienced auditors to include external candidates; (3) Develop and complete the training curriculum before the next hiring wave; (4) Use strategic communications to market the role internally. Retention/success side: (1) Complete PM training program; (2) Address resistance from engagement teams through leadership communications and education about PM value; (3) Ensure PMs are not over-stretched by cross-regional assignments; (4) Develop interim tools/resources for the 40 teams without a PM during the six-month hiring hiatus. Center of Excellence concept can unify both PM and LCS training.

questions.prompt: [2nd level] The other 30 project teams (of the 70 largest) have started assigning project management responsibilities to people within their team instead of waiting on a trained project manager. What are the potential risks and how would you address them?
questions.guidance: Risks: (1) Inconsistent methodology—untrained internal PMs may not follow RDTC PM standards, undermining the whole initiative; (2) Dual roles create strain on staff who are doing PM work on top of audit duties, risking burnout and quality degradation; (3) Audit quality risk—if PM rigor is not maintained on large engagements, penalties from the oversight board are possible; (4) Cultural precedent that PMs are unnecessary or interchangeable with auditors. Mitigation: (1) Provide interim PM toolkits/playbooks for these teams; (2) Have a trained PM serve as a resource/coach in light-touch capacity across multiple teams; (3) Establish minimum standards and check-ins to ensure methodology compliance; (4) Accelerate hiring as soon as busy season ends.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the potential risks of having engagement team members take on project management responsibilities without formal PM training?

categories.name: Quality & Compliance
ideas: Inconsistent application of RDTC Methodology across large engagements
Increased risk of oversight board penalties if PM standards are not met
Audit errors from splitting attention between audit and PM duties

categories.name: People & Culture
ideas: Staff burnout from dual role responsibilities
Erosion of credibility of the formal PM role across the organization
Senior partners may conclude trained PMs are unnecessary, entrenching resistance
Existing trained PMs may feel their role is devalued

categories.name: Process
ideas: No standardized tracking or reporting without trained PMs
Inability to identify bottlenecks or risks using RDTC PM tools
Inconsistent use of LCS across teams without PM to enforce adoption

categories.name: Organizational Change
ideas: Sets a precedent that workarounds to the change initiative are acceptable
Reduces urgency to complete PM hiring
Fragments the change initiative into uncontrolled variants

recommendation: Prioritize leadership alignment first—engage regional presidents and senior partners to become visible champions; without their buy-in, both LCS and PM adoption will continue to stall on the highest-revenue engagements

Deploy LCS to large accounts via a controlled pilot with at least one willing large engagement, then phase the remainder; identify Super Users in each region to provide peer coaching and reduce partner friction

Address the PM hiring gap with a two-track plan: (1) in the immediate term (next six months during hiring freeze), develop interim PM toolkits and light-touch coaching coverage for the 40 unassigned teams; (2) at busy-season end, relaunch hiring with a fully articulated career path, completed training curriculum, and expanded candidate pool including external hires
Establish a Center of Excellence to own both LCS training and RDTC PM onboarding, creating a durable capability rather than a one-time rollout effort
risks: Large-account LCS deployment fails if senior partners remain disengaged—mitigation: executive sponsorship and communications before go-live
Six-month hiring freeze leaves 40 of 70 largest teams without PM oversight during a critical period—mitigation: interim toolkit and coaching
Internal-only recruiting may not fill the pipeline in time—mitigation: open to external candidates in next hiring wave
next_steps: Within 30 days: Conduct leadership alignment sessions with regional presidents and identify PM champions in each region
Within 60 days: Launch LCS pilot on one or two large engagements; develop interim PM toolkit for teams without a PM
Within 90 days: Complete PM training curriculum; begin communications campaign to market PM career path
At busy-season end (~6 months): Relaunch PM hiring with expanded internal and external recruiting; assess LCS pilot results and plan phased rollout to remaining large accounts
